questions.question: A risk assessment reveals that patching a legacy system to close a known vulnerability would cost $250,000, while the maximum expected loss from exploitation is only $40,000. The organization documents this gap and accepts the exposure. Which risk treatment option best describes this decision?
options: Risk transference — the organization shifts financial exposure to a third-party insurer or contractual partner
Risk avoidance — the organization eliminates the asset entirely to remove the vulnerability from the environment
Risk acceptance — the mitigation cost exceeds the expected financial impact, making acceptance cost-effective
Risk mitigation — the organization deploys compensating controls to reduce the probability of exploitation
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance is chosen when the cost of a control exceeds the risk's expected value. Here, spending $250,000 to prevent a maximum $40,000 loss is economically unjustifiable. The organization formally documents acceptance, assigns ownership, and re-evaluates at the next risk review cycle. This is distinct from ignoring risk — accepted risk is tracked and monitored. Risk transference (cyber insurance, contracts) shifts financial impact to a third party. Risk avoidance eliminates the activity or asset. Risk mitigation reduces likelihood or impact through controls.

questions.question: A security team discovers that financial audit records are being automatically purged after 18 months. Applicable regulations require a mandatory 7-year retention period for these records. Which data management requirement is being violated?
options: Data minimization — the organization retains personal data beyond what is necessary for its processing purpose
Data sovereignty — records stored domestically are subject to conflicting foreign jurisdictional requirements
Retention policy compliance — records are being destroyed before the legally mandated retention period expires
Data integrity — the automated deletion process modifies the records' content without documented authorization
questions.explanation: Data retention requirements mandate that certain record types be kept for specified periods to support audits, litigation, and regulatory compliance. Destroying records before the required period violates these obligations and can expose the organization to legal penalties and inability to defend against claims. A compliant retention program includes classification-based schedules, legal hold procedures (which suspend normal purge cycles during litigation), and documented disposal methods (e.g., NIST SP 800-88 for media sanitization). Data minimization is a privacy principle requiring the opposite — collecting and keeping less, not more.

questions.question: A developer stores a SHA-256 hash of each configuration file on a tamper-evident logging server at deployment time. During an audit, a configuration file's computed hash does not match its stored baseline value. Which security property does this hash-comparison control primarily enforce?
options: Confidentiality — the hashing process prevents unauthorized parties from reading the configuration file contents
Availability — the logging server ensures the configuration files remain retrievable during an audit or outage
Integrity — the hash comparison detects whether the file was modified after its baseline value was recorded
Non-repudiation — the stored hash proves the developer authorized the specific configuration at deployment time
questions.explanation: Integrity ensures that data has not been altered in an unauthorized or undetected manner. Cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256) produce a fixed-length digest that changes entirely if even one bit of the source file changes — the avalanche effect. File integrity monitoring (FIM) tools like Tripwire use this principle to detect unauthorized changes to critical files. SHA-256 alone does not provide confidentiality (it does not encrypt) or non-repudiation (a hash does not establish who made a change — digital signatures on the hash would be needed for non-repudiation).

questions.question: A legacy payment service continues negotiating TLS 1.0 sessions because neither the client nor server has been updated to enforce a minimum protocol version. Which attack category is MOST directly enabled by sustained use of TLS 1.0 in this deployment?
options: Session fixation — attackers force clients to adopt a predetermined session token prior to authentication
Protocol downgrade attacks exploiting known TLS 1.0 weaknesses such as BEAST and POODLE cipher vulnerabilities
DNS cache poisoning — the payment service hostname is redirected to a fraudulent server via spoofed DNS records
Certificate revocation bypass — TLS 1.0 clients cannot check OCSP stapling responses to verify certificate validity
questions.explanation: TLS 1.0 uses cipher suites with known cryptographic weaknesses. BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) targets CBC-mode ciphers in TLS 1.0, and POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) can be adapted to TLS 1.0 padding behavior. These attacks exploit the protocol version itself, making a downgrade attack feasible when an attacker can intercept traffic and manipulate negotiation. TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20) and TLS 1.3 eliminate these weaknesses. PCI DSS and NIST SP 800-52 explicitly prohibit TLS 1.0 for payment card data environments.

questions.question: An enterprise deploys SAML 2.0 federation so employees can access SaaS applications with corporate credentials. The identity provider (IdP) issues digitally signed assertions to each service provider (SP). Which security property prevents an attacker who intercepts an assertion from submitting a modified version to gain elevated privileges?
options: Multi-factor authentication — the IdP requires a second factor, so a captured assertion cannot be replayed successfully
Attribute-based access control — the SP evaluates role attributes within each assertion before granting any permissions
Digital signature verification — the SP validates the IdP's signature, detecting any post-issuance tampering with assertion data
Single logout (SLO) — terminating the IdP session simultaneously invalidates all active SP sessions for that user
questions.explanation: In SAML 2.0, the IdP signs assertions using its private key. The SP validates the signature against the IdP's public certificate. Any modification to the assertion — including altering role or group attributes — invalidates the signature, and the SP must reject the tampered assertion. This is the key defense against assertion forgery and privilege escalation via SAML. A well-known attack class, XML Signature Wrapping (XSW), attempts to exploit improper signature validation by moving the signed element while injecting malicious attributes; proper schema validation and XPath-safe signature checking mitigate this.

questions.question: A penetration tester gains shell access to an internal server and then uses that foothold's stored credentials and trust relationships to access additional systems that were not original targets. Which penetration testing phase BEST describes these post-exploitation activities?
options: Reconnaissance — gathering open-source intelligence and network topology data before the initial intrusion
Lateral movement — using a compromised host as a pivot point to extend access across the internal environment
Privilege escalation — obtaining higher permission levels on the originally compromised server's local operating system
Reporting — documenting newly discovered attack paths and out-of-scope systems for the final engagement report
questions.explanation: Lateral movement describes an attacker's actions after initial compromise — using the foothold to access other hosts by exploiting trust relationships, harvested credentials, pass-the-hash, Kerberoasting, or remote execution techniques. It is distinct from privilege escalation (gaining higher rights on the same host) and reconnaissance (pre-compromise information gathering). In a penetration test, lateral movement findings are critical because they reveal the true blast radius of an initial compromise — a single phished user or vulnerable edge device can become the entry point for full domain compromise if network segmentation, credential hygiene, and least privilege controls are absent.

questions.question: Before imaging a server involved in a suspected insider data theft, a forensic investigator photographs the physical device, documents its current state, and records the name, timestamp, and signature of every person who subsequently handles the hardware. What forensic principle do these documentation steps collectively preserve?
options: Order of volatility — capturing the most transient evidence first ensures nothing is lost when the system is powered down
Legal hold — the organization formally suspends automated retention policies to protect evidence from scheduled deletion
Chain of custody — an unbroken, documented record of evidence handling supports its admissibility in legal proceedings
Imaging integrity — cryptographic hashing of the forensic image confirms it is an exact mirror of the original media
questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented chronology of who collected, handled, transferred, and analyzed evidence from the moment of seizure through presentation in court. Any break in the chain — an undocumented handler, a missing timestamp, or an unsecured storage period — can allow the defense to challenge admissibility. Chain of custody is distinct from order of volatility (the sequence in which volatile evidence such as RAM, swap, and disk is captured), legal hold (a directive to suspend routine data destruction), and imaging integrity (hash comparison of source and forensic copy).

questions.question: A web application builds a SQL query by directly concatenating an unvalidated URL parameter into the query string. An attacker submits the value `1; DROP TABLE orders;--` as the parameter and successfully deletes the orders table. Which vulnerability class does this attack represent?
options: Cross-site scripting (XSS) — malicious script in the parameter is reflected into and executed in other users' browsers
Insecure deserialization — the URL parameter value is converted into a harmful object by the application runtime
SQL injection — unvalidated input is interpreted by the database as executable SQL commands rather than as data
Path traversal — the crafted parameter navigates the server's file system to access unauthorized configuration files
questions.explanation: SQL injection occurs when user-supplied data is embedded directly into a SQL query without sanitization or parameterization, allowing the attacker's input to alter the query's logic or structure. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) and stored procedures with bound parameters are the primary defenses — they ensure user input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL. ORMs that use parameterized queries by default also mitigate this. The OWASP Top 10 lists injection as a critical vulnerability category. Stored procedures that still concatenate inputs internally do NOT provide protection.

questions.question: A CISSP-certified professional discovers a colleague is selling proprietary customer data to a competitor in violation of applicable law and company policy. The CISSP's manager instructs them to stay silent to avoid regulatory and financial exposure for the organization. What does the ISC2 Code of Ethics require the CISSP to do?
options: Report the violation to an appropriate authority, because protecting society takes precedence over loyalty to an employer
Follow the manager's directive, because organizational policy and chain of command supersede professional ethics codes
Conduct a confidential internal investigation first, so all facts are confirmed before any external disclosure is made
Seek written legal guidance from the organization's counsel before taking any action that could trigger liability
questions.explanation: The ISC2 Code of Ethics has four canons listed in priority order: (1) Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure. (2) Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally. (3) Provide diligent and competent service to principals. (4) Advance and protect the profession. When canons conflict, higher-numbered canons yield to lower-numbered ones — society (Canon 1) comes before loyalty to an employer (Canon 3). Knowingly remaining silent about illegal conduct violates Canons 1 and 2. The CISSP must report, even if doing so harms the organization's interests or contradicts the manager's preference.

questions.question: A user wants to send a confidential message to a colleague using asymmetric cryptography, ensuring that only the intended recipient can decrypt it. Which key does the sender use for the encryption operation?
options: The sender's private key — the sender encrypts with their own private key so any recipient can verify the source
The sender's public key — the matching private key held by the intended recipient will be used to decrypt the message
The recipient's public key — only the recipient's corresponding private key can decrypt what this public key encrypts
A symmetric session key derived from both parties' key pairs using a Diffie-Hellman key agreement protocol
questions.explanation: In asymmetric (public-key) cryptography, encryption for confidentiality uses the recipient's public key. Only the recipient's corresponding private key can decrypt the ciphertext, ensuring only the intended recipient can read the message. Note the contrast: encrypting with one's own private key (as in digital signing) provides authenticity but NOT confidentiality — anyone with the public key can decrypt. In practice, asymmetric encryption is used to wrap a symmetric session key (hybrid encryption) because symmetric ciphers are far faster for bulk data. RSA-OAEP and ECIES are common hybrid encryption schemes.

questions.question: An organization's CISO is preparing a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) for a Tier-1 application. The team needs to set a value indicating how much data the business can afford to lose in a disaster, measured in time. Which metric represents this?
options: MTBF — mean time between failures, an availability metric for hardware components
RTO — the maximum tolerable time to restore the service after a disruption
RPO — the maximum acceptable age of data at the moment of recovery
MTD — the maximum tolerable downtime before catastrophic business impact
questions.explanation: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) defines the maximum amount of data loss tolerable, expressed as time. An RPO of 15 minutes means backups or replication must capture data at least every 15 minutes; in a disaster, you may lose up to 15 minutes of writes. RTO is the time to recover (a different but related metric). MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime) is the absolute limit before the business cannot survive — RTO must always be less than MTD. MTBF describes how often hardware fails, unrelated to BIA targets.

questions.question: During a vendor risk review, a procurement team discovers a SaaS provider stores customer data in a country with weaker data protection laws than the organization's home jurisdiction. The customer has explicit consent only for processing in the home jurisdiction. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Accept the risk because the SaaS contract includes a generic indemnification clause covering data protection breaches
Renegotiate the contract to require data residency in an approved jurisdiction and obtain documented commitments from the provider
Implement field-level encryption so the provider cannot read the data, eliminating the need to address residency at all
Notify all affected customers individually and request retroactive consent for the secondary processing location
questions.explanation: Data residency requirements driven by consent or regulation (GDPR, LGPD, PIPL) are contractual obligations between the organization and its customers. The correct response is to enforce residency upstream — renegotiate the SaaS contract to require storage in an approved jurisdiction, with documented commitments and audit rights. Indemnification clauses transfer cost but not regulatory liability. Field-level encryption helps with confidentiality but doesn't necessarily address residency, which is about WHERE data physically sits (some regulators treat encrypted data as still 'personal data' if the keys can be recovered). Retroactive consent is rarely a valid legal basis under modern privacy law.

questions.question: An organization classifies a dataset as 'Confidential — Customer Financial'. The data owner mandates encryption at rest, access logging, and a 7-year retention policy. After 7 years, what is the appropriate disposition?
options: Move the data to lower-cost archive storage indefinitely, since storage is cheap and data may have future analytical value
Securely destroy the data per the organization's media-sanitization standard and document destruction in an audit-trail record
Anonymize the data and retain it for analytics, since anonymization removes personal identifiers and regulatory scope
Transfer the data to a less-regulated subsidiary that can retain it under different policies for business intelligence purposes
questions.explanation: Retention policies cut both ways: they specify a minimum AND maximum holding period. After the policy's defined retention horizon, the data MUST be disposed of per the organization's sanitization standard (NIST SP 800-88: Clear, Purge, or Destroy depending on classification). Destruction must be documented in an audit trail — when, how, by whom, witnessed if required. Indefinite retention violates the policy and increases liability. 'Anonymization' is harder than it sounds — combined with other datasets, supposedly anonymous data can be re-identified, so most regulators don't recognize it as exiting scope unless it meets a high bar (e.g., GDPR's 'irreversibly anonymized' standard). Transferring to a subsidiary to evade controls is a compliance violation.

questions.question: An architect is designing a multi-tenant SaaS platform. Each tenant's data must be isolated such that a vulnerability in the application layer cannot leak one tenant's data to another. Which isolation model provides the STRONGEST boundary?
options: Logical isolation via row-level security policies enforced by the shared database engine on every query
Tenant-ID column added to every table, with application code responsible for including the correct tenant filter on each query
Separate database instance per tenant on shared infrastructure, with credentials scoped per tenant at the database layer
Dedicated infrastructure (separate VPC, separate database, separate compute) per tenant, fully isolated at the network layer
questions.explanation: Tenant isolation exists on a spectrum, each step adding cost but reducing blast radius. (a) App-enforced tenant_id filter: cheapest, but a single missed WHERE clause leaks data. (b) Row-level security: database engine enforces filter — eliminates the missed-filter risk but still shares storage and processes. (c) Database-per-tenant on shared infrastructure: separates storage and credentials but shares compute. (d) Fully separate infrastructure: strongest — a compromise of tenant A's stack literally cannot reach tenant B because there is no shared resource to pivot through. Pick the level that matches the data sensitivity: SOC2-grade SaaS usually starts at (b) or (c); regulated industries (healthcare, banking) often require (d).

questions.question: A network team is designing segmentation for a corporate environment that includes a guest WiFi, an employee LAN, a server VLAN, and a regulated PCI cardholder-data zone. Which approach BEST aligns with defense-in-depth principles?
options: Place all four networks behind a single edge firewall and rely on host-based firewalls inside each zone for inter-zone traffic control
Use separate VLANs for each network and rely on the trunk's VLAN tags to provide isolation at Layer 2
Use separate VLANs plus an inspection-capable firewall enforcing explicit allow rules between zones, with the PCI zone receiving the strictest controls and logging
Use a flat Layer-2 network with strong endpoint EDR coverage so any compromised host is immediately detected and isolated
questions.explanation: Segmentation is the practical expression of defense-in-depth at the network layer. The correct pattern combines (1) Layer-2 VLAN separation so broadcast domains don't cross, (2) a Layer-3 firewall (or L3 ACL) enforcing zone-to-zone policy with explicit allow rules and implicit deny, and (3) escalating controls for higher-sensitivity zones — for PCI that means dedicated logging, stricter rules, and reduced ingress paths. A single firewall at the edge can't filter inter-zone traffic. VLAN tagging alone is not a security boundary (VLAN hopping is well-documented). A flat network with EDR is detection-only and violates PCI DSS segmentation requirements.

questions.question: An organization is implementing zero-trust network architecture. Which principle BEST captures the core idea that drives zero-trust design decisions?
options: All traffic inside the corporate network is trusted because the perimeter firewall has already filtered untrusted sources
Trust no entity by default — verify identity, device posture, and authorization on every access request regardless of network origin
Encrypt all traffic with TLS so that even if an attacker is inside the network, they cannot read the data in transit
Eliminate the perimeter firewall entirely since the network is no longer the security boundary in cloud-first environments
questions.explanation: Zero-trust replaces 'trust the network, distrust the internet' with 'trust nothing, verify everything'. Every access request — even from a device sitting in the corporate office on the corporate VLAN — must present identity, device-posture evidence, and authorization scope, evaluated against policy before access is granted. This typically manifests as: identity-aware proxy in front of every application, continuous device attestation, micro-segmentation, just-in-time and just-enough access. TLS-everywhere is supportive but doesn't define zero-trust. Eliminating perimeter firewalls is not zero-trust — you still want defense in depth; you simply no longer treat 'inside' as a trust boundary.

questions.question: A security engineer is implementing privileged access management (PAM) for a Linux server fleet. Administrators currently use a shared root account, with credentials in a wiki. What is the MOST appropriate immediate improvement?
options: Rotate the shared root password monthly and require all administrators to memorize the new password to avoid storage in writing
Implement individual user accounts with sudo privileges, log all sudo invocations, and disable direct root SSH login
Move the shared root password from the wiki into a password manager with access restricted to the operations team
Configure SSH key-based authentication for the shared root account and distribute the same private key to each administrator
questions.explanation: Shared accounts are an accountability gap — when something breaks or gets exfiltrated, the audit log says 'root did it' and you can't trace it back to a person. The PAM-aligned fix is: (1) individual identities per administrator, (2) elevation via sudo on a least-privilege basis, with rules per command/host, (3) full sudo logging shipped off-host, (4) disable root SSH login (`PermitRootLogin no`). This restores accountability AND least-privilege at the same time. Rotating a shared password doesn't fix the accountability gap. Moving it into a password manager improves storage but not attribution. Sharing an SSH key has the same problem as sharing a password — worse, because keys often don't get rotated when someone leaves.

questions.question: An organization needs to grant a contractor access to specific files in a corporate document store. The contractor needs read-only access for 90 days, after which access must end automatically. Which IAM control combination BEST satisfies the requirement with least friction?
options: Create a permanent contractor account; rely on a calendar reminder for the access owner to manually revoke access on day 90
Provision the account in a 'contractors' security group with read-only ACL on the relevant folder; set an account expiration date of 90 days in the directory service
Issue the contractor a copy of a permanent employee's credentials with a verbal agreement to not use them after 90 days
Grant the contractor full administrator rights but instruct them to only access the specific files they need for the engagement
questions.explanation: The control combination needed: (a) least privilege (read-only, scoped folder), (b) authentication tied to a real individual identity (so audit logs are attributable), (c) automatic expiration. Modern directory services (Active Directory, Azure AD, Okta) support setting an account expiration date — at the timestamp, sign-in is denied automatically with no manual step required. This is the LEAST-friction control combination that meets the requirement. Calendar reminders are unreliable. Sharing credentials violates the identity-attribution principle. Over-permissioning (admin rights) violates least privilege and creates audit nightmares.

questions.question: A penetration tester reports a finding to the security team: she discovered a path-traversal vulnerability in the company's customer portal that allows reading arbitrary files on the web server, including configuration files containing database credentials. What is the appropriate severity assessment under a CVSS-aligned framework?
options: Low — the vulnerability requires authentication to exploit and only exposes static configuration files, not active database content
Medium — the vulnerability allows information disclosure but does not directly grant remote code execution
High — the vulnerability discloses database credentials enabling lateral movement, even though it does not directly execute code
Critical — the vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote code execution against the database server through credential disclosure
questions.explanation: Severity is set by exploitability and impact. Path traversal on a public portal that discloses database credentials is High severity even when it does not directly execute code on the database server. The reason: an attacker who reads the credentials can pivot to the database directly with attacker-controlled access — a downstream code-execution / data-exfiltration risk. Calling it 'Critical' would normally require directly-exploitable RCE without a pivot step; calling it 'Medium' would normally require limited info disclosure without credential exposure; 'Low' requires either authentication AND minimal impact, which doesn't apply here.

questions.question: A SOC analyst is investigating a series of failed login attempts against an executive's account. Logs show 12 failures over 4 hours from 7 different geographic locations, then a successful login from an 8th location. The user is on vacation in an entirely different country. Which response action should the analyst take FIRST?
options: Email the user asking whether the activity was theirs, because confirming with the user prevents false-positive disruption
Force a password reset for the account and email the user a new temporary password to use on their next sign-in
Disable the account immediately, revoke active sessions, and escalate per incident-response playbook for suspected account compromise
Continue monitoring the account for additional suspicious activity to gather more evidence before taking any disruptive action
questions.explanation: The signal pattern — distributed failed logins followed by a successful login from a different geographic location while the legitimate user is elsewhere — is highly diagnostic of credential-stuffing or password-spray success. The FIRST action is containment: disable the account, kill active sessions, escalate per playbook. Out-of-band contact with the user comes next, but disabling first prevents an active attacker from causing further damage during minutes of email-back-and-forth. Continuing to monitor lets the attacker exfiltrate data or pivot. Pushing a temp password by email assumes the email account isn't itself compromised — risky.

questions.question: A security architect is selecting a logging strategy for a regulated environment. Auditors require that logs be tamper-evident and retained for 7 years. Which approach BEST satisfies the requirement?
options: Store logs on the same servers that generate them, with file-system permissions denying delete to non-admin users
Ship logs to a centralized SIEM with write-once-read-many (WORM) storage and hash-chained log file integrity validation
Encrypt logs at rest with a customer-managed key, restricting decryption to the audit team for after-the-fact review
Forward logs to a backup service that takes nightly snapshots of the log directory and stores them off-site
questions.explanation: Tamper-evident logging requires that any modification or deletion is detectable. The canonical pattern: centralized log aggregation (so the system being attacked cannot tamper with its own logs), append-only / WORM storage (S3 Object Lock, immutable Blob storage), and integrity validation via hash chains or digital signatures so missing or modified entries are detectable forensically. 7-year retention requires durable archival tier (Glacier, Cool Blob, GCS Archive). Permissioning logs on the source server provides no protection if the server is compromised. Encryption at rest helps confidentiality but does not prevent deletion. Nightly snapshots have an up-to-24-hour gap during which logs can be tampered with.

questions.question: A development team uses a CI/CD pipeline to deploy code to production. The CISO wants to ensure code cannot be modified after security review and before deployment. Which control BEST achieves this?
options: Code review by two senior engineers before merge, with the reviewers signing off in the pull request description
Cryptographic signing of build artifacts after passing CI; the deploy step verifies the signature before promoting to production
Source-code escrow with a third party so any deviation from approved code can be proven against an independent reference
Multi-factor authentication on developer accounts and quarterly access reviews to the source code repository
questions.explanation: Artifact signing creates a cryptographically-verifiable chain of custody between the build (which passed tests + security checks) and the deploy step. The deployer accepts only artifacts signed by the trusted build system; any tampering between build and deploy breaks the signature. Tools: Sigstore/Cosign for OCI images, in-toto for build provenance, SLSA framework for end-to-end attestations. Code review is essential earlier in the pipeline but doesn't protect post-merge artifacts. Source-code escrow is for business continuity, not active integrity. MFA on developer accounts reduces the chance of compromise but doesn't address tampering between build and deploy.

questions.question: A security engineer is reviewing an application's authentication flow. The application stores user passwords using SHA-256 with a per-user salt. What is the MOST significant weakness in this approach for protecting passwords against modern offline attacks?
options: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit output, which is too short to resist quantum-computing attacks expected within the next five years
Per-user salts do not provide enough entropy and should be replaced by a pepper stored in a hardware security module
SHA-256 is a fast, general-purpose hash; modern GPUs compute billions of guesses per second, making brute-force feasible against weak passwords
Salts must be applied before the hash function is selected, and SHA-256 does not natively support salt-aware modes of operation
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is a fast cryptographic hash, designed for performance — exactly the wrong property for password hashing. A modern GPU computes ~10 billion SHA-256 hashes per second; a $20k cracking rig can iterate the most common 99% of passwords in hours, salts notwithstanding (salts prevent rainbow tables, not brute force). Password hashing requires deliberately slow, memory-hard algorithms: Argon2id (winner of the Password Hashing Competition, current recommendation), scrypt, or bcrypt. These are tuned to take ~100-500 ms per hash, making large-scale offline brute force economically impractical. Quantum threat to SHA-256 (which would weaken its preimage resistance) is not the dominant concern; the dominant concern is classical brute force. Peppers add defense in depth but don't fix the speed problem. Salt-aware modes are not a SHA-256 limitation.

questions.question: An application vendor disclosed a critical vulnerability in a library used by a customer-facing web application. The patch is available but requires a full application redeploy. Business operations require the application to be available 24/7. Which approach BEST balances security and availability?
options: Wait for the next quarterly maintenance window in 6 weeks to deploy the patch alongside other planned changes for efficiency
Deploy a WAF rule blocking the known exploit pattern immediately as a compensating control; schedule a coordinated patch deployment within the published SLA for critical vulnerabilities
Take the application offline immediately for the duration of the patch deployment and notify users via a status page banner
Block all incoming traffic to the application until the vendor releases a hotfix that does not require a full redeploy
questions.explanation: Critical vulnerabilities require fast mitigation but not necessarily disruptive patching when a compensating control is available. The standard pattern: (1) deploy a WAF rule, IPS signature, or feature flag to block the specific exploit pattern within minutes — buys time. (2) Schedule the patch within the formal SLA for critical vulnerabilities (typically 24-72 hours). (3) Coordinate with operations for a controlled deployment. Quarterly windows are inappropriate for critical risk. Indiscriminate offline-time violates availability SLAs and is unnecessary when compensating controls exist. Blocking all traffic until a hotfix exists assumes the vendor will produce one quickly, which is rarely true.

questions.question: A new project is in the design phase. The architect is selecting between integrating security review as a separate phase before launch versus building security checks into each design and code-review iteration. Which approach is MOST aligned with secure SDLC best practice?
options: Integrate security review as a single gate immediately before production launch, since this provides a fresh look without iterative bias
Embed security into every SDLC phase — threat modeling at design, SAST/SCA in CI, security review on PRs, DAST in staging, monitoring in production
Run a penetration test once a year after the application is in production, treating findings as the primary security improvement input
Rely on the development team's general security awareness training, with no dedicated security review unless a vulnerability is reported
questions.explanation: Secure SDLC ('shift-left' or DevSecOps) embeds security at every phase, not as a gate before launch. Specific practices per phase: design — threat modeling (STRIDE / PASTA), abuse-case review. Code — SAST scans for known patterns, SCA scans dependencies for CVEs. Build — artifact signing, SBOM generation. Test — DAST against staging, fuzzing for input-handling code. Deploy — admission policies, vulnerability gates. Run — runtime monitoring, log analytics. The reason: finding a flaw at design costs ~$1; finding it post-launch costs ~$100-1000x. Single-gate review pre-launch finds issues too late to fix without rework. Annual pentest is necessary but insufficient. Awareness training is foundational but not a substitute for tooling.
